To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
low concentrations of penicillins (less than the concentration required to saturate their binding sites) cause a rapid cessation of cell division and a decrease in cell size.

low, growth-inhibition concentrations (2.0 to 2.5× MIC) of penicillins immediately halt the exponential increase in peptidogylcan synthesis normally associated with cell multiplication, but allow the rate of pepticoglycan synthesis already in progress at that time to be maintained for 1 to 1.5 h.

low concentrations of penicillins (2.5 to 5.0 times the minimum inhibitory concentrations) immediately halt the exponential increase in rate of peptodiglycan synthesis normally occurring as a result of cell multiplication in a tolerant strain, but allow the rate of pepto-diglycan synthesis occurring when the penicillin was added to be maintained for 1 h.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects on the growth and metabolism of Streptococci of penicillin concentrations which are multiples of the minimum concentration required to inhibit growth.

the effects of penicillin at concentrations below the minimum inhibitory concentrations of the organism, which is a strain of Streptococci mutans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of low, growth-inhibition concentrations of penicillins on Streptococcus FA-1 are not due to a specific effect of penicilline binding to its receptor.
penicillin at low, growth-inhibited concentrations (2.25× the minimum inhibi-tory concentration) does not affect the synthesis of cell envelope components, but it does affect cell morphogenesis.
penicillin G, in low concentrations, inhibits cell division and cell growth but has no immediate effect on the synthesis of peptidylglycan already in progress.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cell wall of Streptococus mutans FA- 1 contains a penicillin-binding protein (PBP-2) which has a very low affinity for penicillin G and which, in the presence of penicillin, is able to synthesize a normal amount of cell wall.

low, growth-inhibition concentrations of penicillins are bacteriostatic, and the inhibition of cell multiplication is caused by the inhibition of the synthesis of new envelope growth areas and not by the inhibition of cell wall synthesis.

penicillin concentrations less than those required for the saturation of the penicillin-binding proteins have the ability to alter cell morphology and to inhibit the synthesis of cell envelope components in a manner similar to the effect of high concentrations of the drug.
The main takeaway from our work is that
low concentrations of penicillins can be very effective at inhibiting the growth of bacteria, even though they do not saturate the specific binding sites for the penicillin on these organisms.
low concentrations of penicillins (less than the minimum inhibitory concentrations) can inhibit the growth of Streptococci without causing any obvious damage to the cell envelope.
the effects of low, subinhibitory concentrations of penicillins on the growth of a tolerant streptococcus strain are not the same as the effects of higher, inhibitory concentrations.
